issues: NG33 (fetched) says single room for suspected infectious pulmonary TB (1.5.1.2), negative pressure if high MDR risk (1.5.1.4), and 3 respiratory samples incl. 1 early morning; it does NOT say 'door kept closed'. why_correct overstated NICE. Key stands (closed door is standard IPC). No live TB-isolation duplicate. Within-batch: PAN4855 is later in draft_all, so this item is kept.

edits.why_correct: A long cough with night sweats, weight loss and upper-zone cavitation is pulmonary tuberculosis until proved otherwise, and it spreads by the airborne route through inhaled droplet nuclei. NICE advises that people with suspected infectious pulmonary TB who stay in hospital are cared for in a single room as a minimum (a negative pressure room if they are at high risk of multidrug-resistant TB), and that several respiratory samples are sent for microscopy and culture so that the diagnosis and drug resistance can be established. Keeping the door closed is standard infection-control practice, because a single room only protects others if it is kept shut. Source: NICE NG33, Tuberculosis, 2016 (updated 2019).

issues: NG60 (fetched) window period 1 month for fourth-generation tests; rec 1.2.5 repeat test past window. 3 weeks is inside window; PEP not in play. No live duplicate. Within-batch: earlier than PAN1987, which duplicates it, so kept. Key neither longest nor shortest.
Standard teaching (Bartonella henselae, kitten scratch, papule then regional node, self-limiting); organism descriptors correct. Citation honestly flagged as standard teaching. No live duplicate.

Key was the shortest option (72) - lengthened. BASHH PID guideline (2018, updated 2019; PDF read): current male partner contacted and offered screening for GC/CT; other recent partners may be offered, tracing within 6 months of symptom onset; empirical (doxycycline) treatment for male partners suggested; avoid sex until patient and partners complete treatment. why_correct overstated ('should' for all recent partners, 'generally six months'); reworded. Not a duplicate of live PID/partner items (OG038, ID033, DS044, DS045 test other points; ID031, BX994, PAQ15837 concern chlamydia/gonorrhoea notification).

options.C: Offer recent partners testing and treatment for chlamydia and gonorrhoea even if well

edits.correct_answer: C. Offer recent partners testing and treatment for chlamydia and gonorrhoea even if well
edits.why_correct: PID is usually caused by sexually transmitted organisms, so her current partner should be contacted and offered testing and treatment for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, and other recent partners (traced back about six months from the onset of her symptoms) may be offered the same, without waiting for her results. This matters because many infected male partners have no symptoms, and it prevents reinfection and onward transmission. She should also avoid sex until she and her partners have completed treatment. Source: BASHH UK national guideline for the management of pelvic inflammatory disease (2018, updated 2019).

issues: UKHSA: scarlet fever notifiable; exclude until at least 24 h after starting appropriate antibiotics; no routine prophylaxis for household contacts; guidance page last updated 3 April 2023 (fetched). 24 h rule is stable. No live duplicate (PED022 diagnosis only).
Anal SCC strongly linked to persistent high-risk HPV, HIV a risk factor; GBMSM HPV vaccination via sexual health services is correct. Distractor explanations accurate. No live duplicate.

Within-batch duplicate of PAN9976 (negative fourth-generation HIV test soon after exposure; repeat after window period). PAN9976 is earlier in draft_all.json order, so this later item is dropped per rule. Clinically sound otherwise.

Clinically sound (adherent bleeding grey pseudomembrane, toxic, unvaccinated = diphtheria; notifiable; antitoxin plus antibiotics without waiting for culture). Citation said guidance 'not fetched'; UKHSA page fetched (Public health control and management of diphtheria in England, updated July 2025) so cite it. Not a duplicate of PAN3824 (transmission only).

edits.why_correct: A tough adherent grey pseudomembrane that bleeds on removal, with a toxic child, neck swelling and an unvaccinated background, is classic for diphtheria caused by toxin-producing Corynebacterium diphtheriae. It is a notifiable disease and needs urgent isolation, public health notification and treatment with antitoxin and antibiotics without waiting for culture confirmation. Source: UKHSA, Public health control and management of diphtheria in England (guidelines, updated 2025).

Clinically correct (HEV genotype 1/2 in endemic areas, third-trimester fulminant risk; UK-acquired genotype 3 does not carry this risk, so the travel history matters). options.E: Hepatitis D virus co-infection with hepatitis B

edits.why_correct: Hepatitis E is spread by the faecal-oral route through contaminated water or food and is common in parts of Asia and Africa. It is usually self-limiting, but in pregnancy, especially the third trimester, infection with the genotypes seen in endemic regions carries a much higher risk of fulminant liver failure and poor fetal outcomes. Source: standard UK teaching on travel-associated viral hepatitis in pregnancy (British Liver Trust, Hepatitis E and pregnancy).
edits.why_wrong: A. Hepatitis C is blood-borne, usually causes a silent infection and has no risk factors here. C. Cytomegalovirus rarely causes marked jaundice in an immunocompetent adult and has no link to untreated water. D. Epstein-Barr virus causes sore throat and lymphadenopathy, with only mild liver enzyme changes. E. Hepatitis D needs hepatitis B to replicate and is spread by blood or sexual contact, not by water.

edits.stem:
An 18-year-old university student attends an out-of-hours GP service with five days of stinging on passing urine and needing to pass urine often. A urine dipstick shows white cells but no nitrites and no blood. Over the last two days she has also had a dull ache low in her abdomen, a new yellow vaginal discharge and pain deep inside during sex. She feels hot and shivery. On examination both sides of the pelvis are tender and moving the cervix is very painful. She had condomless sex with a new partner three weeks ago.

Which diagnosis is most likely?
edits.why_correct: Dysuria and frequency can occur with pelvic inflammatory disease, but lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia, abnormal discharge, fever and cervical motion and adnexal tenderness in a sexually active young woman point to PID, and white cells without nitrites do not make this a urinary infection. Empirical treatment should start without waiting for swab results, alongside a pregnancy test and chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAATs. Source: BASHH, UK national guideline for the management of pelvic inflammatory disease, 2019.
edits.why_wrong: A. A simple lower urinary tract infection does not cause discharge, deep dyspareunia or cervical motion tenderness, and the dipstick lacks nitrites. B. Pyelonephritis gives loin pain, rigors and a higher fever rather than pelvic tenderness. D. Candidiasis causes itching and a thick white discharge without pelvic tenderness or fever. E. A ruptured cyst causes sudden severe pain, usually without fever or discharge.
edits.exam_trap: Urinary symptoms attract the label cystitis, but a discharge and pelvic tenderness on examination point elsewhere.

issues: Content verified against NHS Chickenpox page (avoid newborns/pregnant/immunosuppressed; infectious until all spots have scabbed; spreads by being in the same room and by blister fluid). Key B is the shortest option (88 chars): lengthened slightly. Citation tidied. Not a duplicate: BX771 tests infectious period only, ID018/DR110/DS093 post-exposure management.

options.B: Keep her away from both women until every spot has scabbed over, and tell them to seek advice

edits.correct_answer: B. Keep her away from both women until every spot has scabbed over, and tell them to seek advice
edits.why_correct: Chickenpox can be severe in pregnancy, in newborns and in people with weakened immunity, so contact with these groups should be avoided while the child is infectious, until all the spots have formed scabs. A non-immune pregnant woman or an immunosuppressed person who has been in contact should seek urgent medical advice, as prophylaxis may be offered. Source: NHS, Chickenpox, 2025.

issues: Time-sensitive PEPSE assessment is sound (BHIVA/BASHH 2021 guideline: start as soon as possible, ideally within 72 hours; offered by risk assessment). Stem did not say which role in anal sex; BASHH recommends considering PEPSE for receptive anal sex with a partner of unknown status from a higher-prevalence group, so 'receptive' added. Citation admission replaced with proper reference. Different setting from live occupational PEP items (ID024, PAQ11795, BX490); learning point overlap is the urgency of PEP but exposure and scenario differ.

edits.stem:
A 28-year-old man attends a walk-in centre on Saturday morning. The previous night he had condomless receptive anal sex with a casual male partner whose HIV status is unknown. He feels well and asks whether anything can be done to lower his chance of infection.

What is the most appropriate action?
edits.why_correct: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis after sexual exposure (PEPSE) works best when started as soon as possible after the exposure, so he should be assessed urgently, on the same day, rather than waiting for a routine appointment. The decision depends on the type of exposure and the likelihood that the partner has HIV, and a baseline HIV test is taken with follow-up testing afterwards. Out of hours, this means a sexual health clinic or emergency department. Source: BHIVA/BASHH, UK guideline for the use of HIV post-exposure prophylaxis, 2021.

issues: Diagnosis and distractors sound (grouped vesicles, pain, axillary node, no pus, unprotected oral contact; do not incise). Citation carried an admission of non-verification; replaced with plain teaching source. Key is neither longest nor shortest. No live herpetic whitlow item.

edits.why_correct: Grouped clear vesicles with severe pain on a swollen fingertip, after unprotected contact with oral secretions, is typical of herpetic whitlow, a herpes simplex virus infection entering through the skin. Regional lymphadenopathy and mild fever are common and there is no collection of pus. Source: standard UK clinical teaching on herpes simplex virus infection.

issues: Clinically sound (TBM: subacute, cranial nerve VI palsy, lymphocytic CSF, high protein, low glucose). Cueing: stem said 'tuberculosis' and only the key contains the word; stem reworded. Citation admission replaced. No live TBM item.

edits.stem:
A 38-year-old man who moved to the UK from sub-Saharan Africa two years ago has had five weeks of worsening headache, low-grade fevers, night sweats and weight loss. He has become increasingly drowsy and now has a right sixth cranial nerve palsy. Lumbar puncture shows a lymphocytic cerebrospinal fluid with a high protein and a low glucose.

Which organism is the most likely cause?
edits.why_correct: A slowly progressive meningitic illness over weeks, with systemic features such as night sweats and weight loss, cranial nerve palsies and lymphocytic CSF with high protein and low glucose, points to tuberculous meningitis. This is a subacute rather than hyperacute meningitis, and risk is higher with origin in a high-prevalence country. Source: standard UK clinical teaching on central nervous system tuberculosis (management in NICE NG33).

issues: Chlamydia is the most commonly identified cause of non-gonococcal urethritis; scant mucoid discharge with 1-3 week incubation fits. Citation admission replaced. Key not longest/shortest. No live item tests chlamydia vs gonorrhoea discharge character (ID032/ID045 gonorrhoea treatment, BX993 NAAT, ID031 female chlamydia).

edits.why_correct: Mild dysuria with scanty clear or mucoid discharge, an incubation of one to three weeks and unprotected sex with a new partner fit non-gonococcal urethritis, for which Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common identified cause. Gonorrhoea more typically gives an abrupt profuse purulent discharge, though both need NAAT testing and partner notification. Source: BASHH, UK national guideline on the management of non-gonococcal urethritis.

issues: Clinically correct (NG60 1.2.2: confirmatory serology if POCT reactive; referral pathway specialist preferably within 48 h, certainly within 2 weeks - both verified on NICE site). Fix only the citation: it was not tied to the confirmatory-testing recommendation. No live duplicate: PAN7231 starts after confirmation; PAN427 is indicator-condition testing with consent; no live item on a reactive POCT.

edits.why_correct: Point-of-care tests have reduced specificity and sensitivity compared with fourth-generation laboratory tests, so false positives occur and a reactive result needs confirmation by serological testing. NICE advises that people who test positive are then seen by an HIV specialist, preferably within 48 hours and certainly within 2 weeks. Source: NICE NG60, HIV testing: increasing uptake among people who may have undiagnosed HIV, 2016 (point-of-care testing and referral pathway recommendations).

issues: Clinically sound (early congenital syphilis: snuffles, copper palm/sole rash, hepatosplenomegaly at weeks 2-8; distractor descriptions accurate; NHS syphilis page confirms congenital transmission and antenatal screening). why_correct source line contained meta text '(not re-fetched)'; replaced with a clean citation. No live congenital syphilis item (PAN2319 congenital rubella, PAN5690 congenital CMV, ID034/PAQ14794 acquired syphilis).

edits.why_correct: Treponema pallidum crosses the placenta, and untreated maternal syphilis causes congenital syphilis. Early features include persistent nasal discharge (snuffles), a rash involving the palms and soles, hepatosplenomegaly and bone changes, and later features include dental and skeletal abnormalities. Antenatal screening and treatment of the mother is the means of prevention. Source: NHS syphilis guidance (congenital syphilis) and UK antenatal infectious diseases screening programme, with standard paediatric teaching.

edits.why_correct: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the commonest cause of community-acquired pneumonia in adults, classically presenting with abrupt fever, pleuritic chest pain, rust-coloured sputum and lobar consolidation. Severity is then assessed with a score such as CURB65 and empirical antibiotics follow local guidance. Source: NICE NG250, Pneumonia: diagnosis and management, 2025 (severity assessment); the organism is standard teaching.

edits.why_correct: Group A streptococcal pharyngitis can be followed by an immune-mediated complication, acute rheumatic fever, and a full course of an appropriate antibiotic reduces that risk. This is a main reason to complete the course even when symptoms settle. Source: standard teaching on post-streptococcal complications; NICE NG84, Sore throat (acute): antimicrobial prescribing, 2018, for antibiotic choice and course length.

edits.stem:
A 71-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with rigors, new confusion and a high temperature two days after a urinary catheter was inserted. His heart rate and respiratory rate are raised and he is hypotensive. Sepsis is suspected and IV antibiotics have been prescribed. A nurse is ready to take blood cultures.

What is the best approach to the blood cultures?
edits.why_correct: Blood cultures and other microbiological samples should be taken before the first antibiotic dose, because prior antibiotics reduce the yield and the result allows treatment to be narrowed later. However, sampling must never cause a significant delay to antibiotics in a patient with suspected sepsis, who should be treated as an emergency. Source: NICE NG253, Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over, 2025 (recommendation 1.8.1, take microbiological and blood samples before giving an antimicrobial).

edits.stem:
A 21-year-old woman attends a sexual health clinic because her male partner was told yesterday that he has non-gonococcal urethritis. She feels completely well, with no discharge, dysuria, bleeding or pelvic pain, and her abdomen is soft and non-tender.

Which infection is she most likely to be carrying, which if missed can ascend to cause pelvic inflammatory disease and tubal infertility?
edits.why_correct: Chlamydia is the commonest bacterial sexually transmitted infection in the UK, and most infected women have no symptoms, so a partner with non-gonococcal urethritis is an important prompt to test and treat her. Left untreated it can ascend to cause pelvic inflammatory disease, which may lead to ectopic pregnancy and tubal infertility. Testing is by a nucleic acid amplification test, with treatment and partner notification through sexual health services. Source: NHS website, Chlamydia (symptoms and complications), with standard sexual health teaching.
